name: The Ghost Fleet

detectability.signature: Massive organic debris field; residual bioelectric signatures; intermittent life signs from corpse material

proximity: Sensors detect thousands of organic masses ranging from shuttle to dreadnought scale
Bioelectric fields interfere with sensitive equipment
Occasional automated responses from dormant systems
contact: Dead bio-ships may respond to presence with reflexive actions
Parasitic organisms inhabiting corpses may investigate visitors
Risk of disturbing something not entirely dead
prolonged_exposure: Risk of triggering defense reflexes in dormant vessels

age: Estimated 8,000 years (battle date extrapolated from decay)

behavior.cycle: Periodic bioelectric surges as corpses decay

phenomena: Organic signatures on sensors across vast area
Electromagnetic patterns resembling neural activity in some corpses
hazards: Attack by defense reflexes in not-quite-dead vessels
opportunities: Exotic matter collection from preserved bio-components
known_incidents: Research team Delta-7 awakened dormant defense systems in a bio-cruiser corpse in 2867, losing two members before the vessel's reflexes subsided
Xenoarchaeologist Dr. Amara Okonkwo recovered a mostly-intact navigation ganglion that, when stimulated, displayed star charts to unknown regions
description: The Ghost Fleet stretches across three astronomical units of slowly decaying wonder—the remains of thousands of vessels grown rather than built, their organic hulls now drifting tombs of an unknown civilization. The ships range from fighter-analogues smaller than shuttles to leviathans kilometers long, their designs suggesting a species that cultivated vessels like crops, shaping living tissue into weapons of war. Eight thousand years of drift has scattered the fleet, but the scale of destruction remains evident: this was an apocalyptic battle, and these were the losers.

The corpses are not entirely dead. Bioelectric fields still pulse through preserved neural tissue; defense systems occasionally activate in response to proximity; and ecosystems of parasitic organisms have colonized the decay, creating pockets of hostile life within the graveyard. Explorers report movement in peripheral vision, automated responses to stimuli, and in one documented case, a bio-cruiser's weapons organ discharging at a survey vessel that approached too aggressively. The ships remember their purpose, even if their crews are long dust.

No records exist of the species that grew these vessels, or of the enemy they fought. The Ghost Fleet simply appeared in survey records once humanity reached this region of space, its history lost with its creators. Analysis of the bio-technology suggests capabilities beyond current human science: self-repairing hulls, weapons grown from specialized organs, and propulsion systems that may have operated on principles still not understood. The battle that created this graveyard was fought with technologies that would revolutionize human capability, if they could be reverse-engineered.

The Ghost Fleet draws researchers, salvagers, and the merely curious. Xenoarchaeological teams carefully extract preserved components, hoping to understand the bio-engineering that created these vessels. Military interests study weapons systems that, even degraded, outperform modern equivalents. And somewhere within the graveyard, according to persistent rumors, at least one ship remains functional—damaged but not dead, waiting for a crew that will never return. Whether this vessel represents opportunity or threat depends on who finds it first, and whether they can convince it they're friends.
